name: Quantified self

lead: Quantified self means recording personal data such as weight, steps, sleep, food and lab markers. For appearance, the payoff comes through feedback: tracking helps people see whether training, diet or sleep changes are moving their physique.

The term was coined in San Francisco in 2007 by Wired editors Gary Wolf and Kevin Kelly. Systematic reviews of self-tracking report benefits for motivation and behaviour in some groups, with the need for more validation.

paras: People use wearables, apps, scales, photos and spreadsheets, reviewing trends weekly. Looksmaxxers often track bodyweight, lifts, sleep and progress photos.
Privacy of data, time burden, and over-reliance on numbers are discussed; the data can be misread without health literacy.

angle.text: Tracking gives feedback on whether routines are working, so people adjust training and diet.

lead: Quantified self is a movement and practice of self-tracking, 'self-knowledge through numbers'. The term was coined in 2007 by Wired editors Gary Wolf and Kevin Kelly, and the first international conference was held in Mountain View in 2011.[1]

Looksmaxxers use it to monitor the inputs that shape appearance - training load, body weight, sleep, nutrition - and compare them with progress photos or measurements. The chain runs from tracking to better-informed habits to physique change.

A 2021 systematic review of 67 studies found research on end users, patients and clinicians covering motivation, goal setting and effects of tracking.[2] A 2020 review argued theory for self-quantification systems is too abstract and needs empirical validation.[3]

paras: Fitness and sleep wearables such as Fitbit and Apple Watch made self-tracking mainstream; practitioners also use glucose monitors, DIY tools and manual logs.[1]
Critics raise data privacy, 'data fetishism' that oversimplifies health, limited health literacy for interpreting data, and the burden of tracking.[1]

A systematic review of 67 empirical studies mapped how self-tracking is used for health and well-being.[2] A review of digital biomarkers found most remain in early validation, with continuous glucose monitoring the clearest success.[4] None of these test appearance outcomes directly.
